newsitem.title: FRANCE: Critical France cancels sell-off of CIC.
newsitem.headline: Critical France cancels sell-off of CIC.

text.p: France called off the sale of regional banking group CIC on Thursday and criticised the heads of the bank and its state-owned parent insurer GAN for failing to help with the privatisation.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announced the cancellation of a sell-off tender launched in August, which drew offers from BNP and Societe Generale, but said that he was determined that the CIC group would be sold off eventually.
"After serious reflection the government has decided to call off the privatisation process for CIC," Arthuis said.

"It seemed important that everyone had the necessary time for reflection," he told a news conference on the sale of 67 percent of CIC shares with a book value of about 9.4 billion francs ($1.85 billion).
"The managers of GAN and CIC did not behave in a way to encourage progress in this process," Arthuis said.
He said he had decided to abandon the privatisation process, which ran into opposition from staff and local politicians, but the government remained determined to sell CIC in the future.
"There is no question of not privatising CIC," he said.
CIC, or Credit Industriel et Commercial, still needed to link up with a group capable of providing it with the funds it needed to develop, Arthuis said.
GAN would also have to be sold, although he said he did not think the market could absorb the sale of GAN and CIC together.
Arthuis suggested it would be difficult to sell GAN before CIC since this would oblige the state to take full control of the banking group.
BNP said it regretted the government's decision to call off the sale, but declined to say whether it would make a fresh offer. Societe Generale declined comment.
CIC said it had no comment.
The privatisation tender launched in the summer carried a list of terms and conditions which suitors had to respect, including respect for CIC's regional integrity.
CIC is a profitable group of group of 11 regional banks whose main customers are medium and large companies and whose sell-off was seen as a prerequisite for the sale of GAN itself.
Arthuis said France's independent privatisation commission had ruled that an offer by Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP) complied with the government's terms and conditions.

But it had rejected the offer from Societe Generale which had suggested buying CIC in two stages -- whereas the government wanted it sold all at once. Societe Generale had not given a firm price, Arthuis said.
Arthuis said he had been concerned there was only one offer on the table for CIC after the privatisation commission verdict.
CIC chairman Bernard Yoncourt infuriated Arthuis in October after declaring on television that the bids could spell the "death" of his regional banking network.
Arthuis replied then: "It is unacceptable coming from a chairman and I shall draw the consequences". On Thursday he declined to be drawn on whether Yoncourt would be replaced.
French press said in the wake of the fracas that it was the intervention of GAN chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud which avoided Yoncourt being fired.
The CIC sale had sparked strikes by staff to highlight their fears of job losses and a break-up of the regional banking group and raised concern among local politicians.
Arthuis said that the privatisation process had been "completely abandoned" and the whole procedure would now have to be started again from scratch.
In theory both BNP and Societe Generale could submit new offers for CIC, while analysts said savings bank grouping Caisses d'Epargne, could also be brought in through a new privatisation tender.
